chief_complaint: profuse projectile vomiting, lethargy, and pale clammy skin 2 hours after feeding in infant
hpi_details: 7-month-old infant presenting with repetitive severe vomiting, pallor, and dehydration precisely 2 hours after first introduction of cow's milk or oat cereal without cutaneous hives or wheezing.
ideas: The mother thinks her baby contracted a violent stomach bug from his older sibling or suffered acute food poisoning from a contaminated batch of cereal.
concerns: She is worried that the severe fluid loss will cause fatal dehydration or brain damage because he became so pale and unresponsive.
expectations: She hopes to receive intravenous fluids for her baby and a clear list of safe foods she can introduce without risking another reaction.
social_hx: 7-month-old infant; lives at home with both parents and an older sibling; no smokers in the household; attends no daycare; formula- and breast-fed with solids introduced from 6 months

clinical_knowledge.topic: Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management of an acute episode is IV fluid resuscitation for dehydration/shock (ondansetron may help with acute vomiting), strict avoidance of the trigger food, and specialist-supervised reintroduction later, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: profuse projectile vomiting, lethargy, and pale clammy skin 2 hours after feeding in infant

Key HPI features: 7-month-old infant presenting with repetitive severe vomiting, pallor, and dehydration precisely 2 hours after first introduction of cow's milk or oat cereal without cutaneous hives or wheezing.
Objective/Exam findings: Lethargic, pale, and clammy with signs of dehydration; no urticaria, angioedema, or wheeze; abdomen soft without peritoneal signs.
Relevant background/PMH: No significant chronic medical history
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Sepsis / serious bacterial infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Lethargy and pallor severe enough to look like shock.
management_principles: Give IV fluid resuscitation for dehydration/shock (ondansetron may help acute vomiting) and strictly avoid the trigger food
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome FPIES: profuse projectile vomiting, lethargy, and pale clammy skin 2 hours after feeding in infant. 7-month-old infant presenting with repetitive severe vomiting, pallor, and dehydration precisely 2 hours after first introduction of cow's milk or oat cereal without cutaneous hives or wheezing.
reference_soap.objective: Lethargic, pale, and clammy with signs of dehydration; no urticaria, angioedema, or wheeze; abdomen soft without peritoneal signs.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome (FPIES) triggered by cow's milk or oat cereal.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Give IV fluid resuscitation for dehydration/shock; ondansetron may help with acute repetitive vomiting. 2. Strictly avoid the trigger food; do not attempt epinephrine or antihistamines, which do not treat this non-IgE-mediated reaction. 3. Refer to allergy/immunology or pediatric GI for confirmation and a supervised plan for future food reintroduction and oral food challenges.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Food Protein-Induced Enterocolitis Syndrome FPIES
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for profuse projectile vomiting, lethargy, and pale clammy skin 2 hours after feeding in infant
Select appropriate laboratory and imaging studies for allergy_immunology
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: A non-IgE-mediated food allergy in infants causing delayed, repetitive vomiting and lethargy 1-4 hours after a trigger food, without hives or wheeze, that can mimic sepsis.
red_flags: Lethargy and pallor severe enough to look like shock
Repeated episodes on re-exposure to the same food

must_ask.say: How long after the feeding did the vomiting start?
Was this a new food being introduced for the first time — milk, cereal, or something else?

must_ask.objective: Absence of typical allergic skin/airway signs
must_ask.say: Did the baby have any hives, swelling, or wheezing, or was it just vomiting?
How pale or floppy did the baby become during the episode?

must_ask.objective: Prior episodes with the same food
must_ask.say: Has this happened before with the same food?

history.answer: My baby started throwing up violently about two hours after eating, and now he is completely pale, limp, and weak.
Everything began suddenly this morning, exactly two hours after his morning feed.
I fed him oat cereal prepared with cow's milk for the very first time around 8:00 AM.
He was completely fine right after eating, but the vomiting started precisely two hours later at 10:00 AM.
He threw up repetitively five or six times in a row, shooting out forcefully across his high chair.
At first it was the cereal and milk he had eaten, but then it became clear watery fluid and yellowish liquid with no blood.
He had one loose, watery bowel movement about an hour after the vomiting started, but no blood in his diaper.
He cried and drew his legs up like his tummy hurt right before throwing up, but now he is too tired to cry.
No, he has not had any fever at all, and his skin actually feels cool.
No, I checked his entire body and there are no hives, red spots, or swelling around his lips or eyes.
He is breathing a little fast, but he is not wheezing, gasping, coughing, or choking.
He has become extremely sleepy and limp, like a ragdoll, and he barely opens his eyes when we call his name.
He turned very pale and grayish, and his hands and feet feel cold and sweaty.
He cannot keep any breast milk or water down, his mouth is dry, and his diaper has been completely dry for six hours.
No, this was his very first time ever tasting oat cereal or cow's milk.
No, he has had no falls, head bumps, or any injuries whatsoever.
No one else at home is sick, and neither my husband, older child, nor I have any stomach trouble.
He usually breastfeeds well along with some purees, and his weight gain has always been on track.
He has been healthy and has no chronic medical conditions or health problems.
He has never been admitted to a hospital and has never had surgery.
He takes no prescription medicines or over-the-counter drugs, only daily vitamin D drops.
He has no known allergies to any medicines.
He was born full-term by normal vaginal delivery with no complications in the nursery.
All of his vaccinations are up to date through six months, and his pediatrician said his growth is normal.
My husband has mild seasonal allergies in the spring, but no one in our family has severe food allergies or gastrointestinal diseases.
He stays home with me and does not go to daycare or nursery.
I thought maybe he caught a terrible stomach virus from his older brother or got food poisoning from a spoiled box of oat cereal.
I'm terrified that he will get dangerously dehydrated or suffer brain damage because he turned so pale and limp right in my arms.
I'm hoping you can give him IV fluids to get his energy back and give me a safe feeding guide so I know what is okay to give him.

exam.finding: Tachycardic at 160 beats per minute, blood pressure 72/46 mmHg, afebrile at 36.2°C, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Lethargic, limp infant lying still, appearing pale, clammy, and noticeably dehydrated.
Pale, cool, and clammy skin with delayed capillary refill of 3 seconds; no urticaria, flushing, or petechial rash.
Eyes appear mildly sunken with absent tearing; pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light.
Dry oral mucosa and dry lips, with no swelling of the lips, tongue, or pharynx.
Clear breath sounds throughout both lung fields with no wheezes, stridor, or crackles.
Tachycardic rhythm with regular rate, normal heart sounds, and no audible murmur.
Weak, thready radial and dorsalis pedis pulses bilaterally; femoral pulses are present.
Abdomen is flat and symmetrical with no visible distension, peristaltic waves, or surgical scars.
Normal bowel sounds heard throughout all four quadrants.
Abdomen is soft, non-distended, and non-tender throughout with no palpable olive-shaped mass or organomegaly.
Supple neck without nuchal rigidity, and the anterior fontanelle is flat to slightly depressed.
Lethargic and drowsy; opens eyes briefly to loud voice and withdraws weakly to gentle touch.
